justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with modest upward drift over longer horizons. For the one-day estimate of 571, I was anchoring closely to the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, assuming mean-reverting behavior over a very short window with minimal directional bias. The one-week estimate of 574 incorporates a slight positive drift, consistent with the general long-run tendency of equity markets to trend upward over time, while still being heavily influenced by the starting price. The one-month estimate of 578 extends that same modest drift assumption further, reflecting the compounding of a small expected return over roughly 21 trading days. The incremental increases across horizons are intentionally small because short-term equity price forecasting has very limited predictive power, and I didn't want to overweight any directional thesis.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated primarily using historical volatility as the backbone. Daily equity index volatility tends to run in the range of 0.8% to 1.2% annualized to the daily scale, so a roughly ±2% band for the one-day horizon seemed consistent with observed market behavior under normal conditions. As the horizon extends to one week and one month, I widened the intervals proportionally using a square-root-of-time scaling approach, which is a standard assumption under random walk models. The one-month interval of roughly ±13% around the point estimate reflects the accumulated uncertainty over a longer period, capturing the reality that a lot can happen in 30 days.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include macroeconomic surprises such as an unexpected inflation print, a central bank policy shift, or a sudden deterioration in credit markets. Geopolitical shocks, earnings surprises from major index constituents, or a liquidity event in financial markets could also cause sharp moves that my confidence intervals would not fully contain. These intervals are calibrated for typical market conditions and implicitly assume no regime change or tail event.

It's worth noting that my intervals, while seemingly wide at longer horizons, are still likely to understate true uncertainty in practice. Fat tails in equity return distributions mean that extreme moves occur more frequently than a normal distribution would suggest. A severe risk-off episode or unexpected policy reversal could easily produce a move of 10–15% or more in a single month, placing realized outcomes well outside my stated 90% confidence band.
